It extends Node's request object with information such as route parameters, query values, headers, the request body, HTTP method, and references to the application and response; body data requires body-parsing middleware.

keyPoints: `req` represents the incoming HTTP request and exposes request-specific data to middleware and route handlers.

Use `req.method` to inspect whether the request uses methods such as GET, POST, or PUT.

The response and request objects expose the same application instance through `res.app` and `req.app`.
Application settings can be read through the returned app object, such as with `res.app.get()`.
Comparing `res.app` with `req.app` confirms that both references identify the same application.

res.statusCode.explanation: `res.statusCode` is the Node.js response property available on Express’s response object. Assign an HTTP status number before the response is sent; Express and Node.js then use it as the response status. For Express’s chainable alternative, use `res.status(code)`.

useCases.title: Control error responses

useCases.title: Access built-in response properties
useCases.scenario: Use Node.js response fields directly when Express does not provide a dedicated helper.

keyPoints: Express exposes Node’s response properties through its enhanced `res` object.
Built-in Node.js response fields and methods are available on `res`.
`res.statusCode` represents the HTTP status code returned for the response.
`res.status(code)` provides Express’s chainable way to set the same status.
gotchas: Use a valid HTTP status code; some Node.js versions throw when the value is invalid.
Keep the value within the 100–599 range.

res.statusMessage.summary: `res.statusMessage` is the HTTP reason phrase associated with the response status code. In Express, use documented response methods such as `res.status()` to select the status; the corresponding message is part of the HTTP response metadata.
res.statusMessage.explanation: `res.statusMessage` is the HTTP response’s reason phrase associated with its status code. Express documentation does not define it as a separate Express method or property; Express response behavior sets the corresponding message when a status is selected, while `res.status()` is the documented API for changing the status.

useCases.scenario: Returning a standard status phrase as text

useCases.scenario: Handling an unknown or custom status code

keyPoints: `res.statusMessage` belongs to the HTTP response represented by Express’s `res` object.
A status code has a registered message, but the documented method that sends that message as text is `res.sendStatus()`.
`res.sendStatus(statusCode)` uses the status code’s registered message as the response body.
An unknown code has no registered status message, so `res.sendStatus()` falls back to the code number in the body.
gotchas: Do not confuse the status message with the response body: `res.sendStatus()` uses the registered message as the body.
Unknown status codes do not provide a registered message; `res.sendStatus()` sends only the numeric code as the body.

res.type.summary: res.type() sets the response Content-Type using either a MIME type or a file extension. MIME types are used literally; extensions are resolved through Express’s MIME mapping.
res.type.explanation: Call res.type(type) to set the response Content-Type. A value containing a slash is treated as a complete MIME type; otherwise Express interprets it as a file extension and looks up the corresponding MIME type.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: A MIME type or a file extension used to determine the response Content-Type.

keyPoints: The method sets the response's Content-Type header based on the supplied value.
The argument may be either a MIME type or an extension.
Without a slash, Express performs a MIME lookup for the extension.
The .html extension resolves to text/html.
The json extension resolves to application/json.
gotchas: Values without a slash are interpreted as extensions, so use a full MIME type when you need an exact header value.

Router.summary: `express.Router([options])` creates a modular, mountable routing and middleware object. Configure parameter inheritance, case sensitivity, and trailing-slash matching with its options.
Router.explanation: `express.Router([options])` creates an independent routing and middleware object. Add router-level middleware and HTTP-method handlers to it, then mount it with `app.use()` or another router’s `use()` method. Options control case sensitivity, strict trailing-slash matching, and whether parent parameters remain available.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration object. `caseSensitive` enables case-sensitive matching and defaults to false; `mergeParams` preserves parent `req.params` and was added in v4.5.0+; `strict` enables strict routing and defaults to false.

useCases.title: Custom matching behavior
useCases.scenario: Control URL matching rules for a router independently of the main application.

keyPoints: A Router combines route definitions with middleware behavior.
Use a Router to isolate a focused section of an application's routing system.
Mount a Router on an application or another Router with `use()`.
Construct one with `express.Router([options])`.
After construction, register middleware and methods such as `get`, `post`, and `put`.
Set `mergeParams: true` when child routes need parameters captured by the parent mount path.
gotchas: Strict routing is off by default, so a trailing slash normally does not change route matching.
Multiple route callbacks run like middleware; each must either complete the response or continue the chain.

RouterOptions.summary: RouterOptions is the optional configuration object for express.Router(). It controls case sensitivity, trailing-slash handling, and inheritance of route parameters from a parent router.
RouterOptions.explanation: RouterOptions is the options object accepted by express.Router(). It controls route matching and parameter inheritance: caseSensitive distinguishes path letter case, strict distinguishes trailing slashes, and mergeParams preserves parameters supplied by a parent router, with child values taking precedence on conflicts.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration object for router behavior.

parameters.name: caseSensitive
parameters.description: Whether route matching distinguishes uppercase and lowercase path characters. Default: false.

parameters.name: mergeParams
parameters.description: Whether to preserve req.params values from the parent router. Default: false.

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Whether route matching distinguishes a path from the same path with a trailing slash. Default: false.

useCases.scenario: Keep `/Foo` and `/foo` as distinct route paths.

useCases.title: Use strict routing
useCases.scenario: Require or reject trailing slashes consistently in route paths.

useCases.title: Merge parent parameters
useCases.scenario: Access parameters captured by a parent router inside a child router.

keyPoints: RouterOptions is an optional object used to configure how the router behaves.
caseSensitive enables case-sensitive route matching when set to true.
mergeParams carries route parameters from a parent router into the child router.
strict enables strict route matching, making trailing slashes significant.
express.Router() returns a new Router instance that can be mounted and used as middleware.
gotchas: When mergeParams is enabled, a child router's parameter overrides a parent router parameter with the same name.
caseSensitive defaults to false, so route paths differing only by letter case match equivalently.
strict defaults to false, so a trailing slash does not distinguish these two paths.

serveStatic.summary: Creates middleware that serves static files from a specified root directory. Missing files pass to the next middleware, enabling fallbacks and middleware stacking.
serveStatic.explanation: serveStatic creates middleware that maps the request URL onto a file below a chosen root directory. If the file is missing, the middleware calls next() so later middleware can handle the request; directory requests use index.html by default unless configured otherwise.

parameters.name: root

parameters.description: Optional configuration controlling static-file serving behavior, such as index, extensions, and setHeaders.

The requested URL is combined with root to locate the file.
Unmatched requests continue through the middleware chain.

When extension fallbacks are configured, the first existing candidate is returned.
Directory URLs resolve to index.html by default.

Directory requests serve index.html unless the index option changes or disables that behavior.
A custom setHeaders function must make header changes synchronously.

strict routing.summary: The `strict routing` application setting controls whether `/foo` and `/foo/` are treated as different routes. When enabled, trailing slashes matter; otherwise, the router treats both forms as equivalent.

trust proxy.summary: `trust proxy` tells Express whether and how to trust a front-facing proxy’s `X-Forwarded-*` headers. Configure it with a boolean, trusted address or subnet, hop count, array, or custom function.
trust proxy.explanation: Set the application’s `trust proxy` value when Express runs behind a known reverse proxy. The setting controls whether Express accepts `X-Forwarded-*` information and how it derives client IP, hostname, and protocol values; use a boolean, trusted address or subnet, hop count, or custom function that matches the deployment topology.

keyPoints: The setting accepts a boolean, address or subnet value, hop count, custom function, or array.
Proxy trust is disabled by default.
Enabling it lets Express use forwarded headers when deriving connection and client IP information.
A true value treats the leftmost forwarded address as the client IP.
A false value treats the application as directly internet-facing and avoids trusting forwarded client information.
A numeric value trusts a fixed number of proxy hops.
Express delegates proxy-address trust evaluation to the `proxy-addr` package.

When proxy trust is enabled, forwarded host information may be client-controlled unless the proxy overwrites it.
Client IP resolution stops at the first untrusted address, so an incorrect trust boundary can produce an incorrect `req.ip`.
